This petition having been heard and reserved, coming on for pronouncement this day, the court pronounced the following:
 ORDER
Since pleadings are complete and learned counsel for the parties are ready to argue the matter finally, therefore, at their joint request, it is heard finally.

2. By this petition filed under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, the petitioner-Bank is assailing the order dated 20.04.2010 (Annexure-P/12) passed by the Central Government Industrial Tribunal (CGIT) [hereinafter referred to as 'the Tribunal'] holding the enquiry conducted by the petitioner-Bank vitiated and permitting the parties to lead evidence so also the final award passed by the Tribunal on 27.06.2014 (Annexure-P/16).

sentences.text: Learned counsel for the petitioner-Bank submits that the respondent-workman was charge-sheeted alleging therein that while performing the duties, he not only committed irregularities, but by misappropriating the amount of Bank and fabricating the documents, he played fraud with the Bank.

He submits that the disciplinary authority, after conducting the enquiry,
held that out of five, four charges were found proved against the delinquent and as such, inflicted the punishment of dismissal from service upon him.

Thereafter, the said order has been assailed by the employee by filing an appeal before the appellate authority and the appellate authority affirming the finding given by the disciplinary authority has dismissed the appeal and as such, the delinquent approached the Tribunal.

4. However, the Tribunal vide order dated 20.04.2010 (Annexure- P/12), had held the enquiry conducted against the employee vitiated and parties were given an opportunity to lead evidence to prove the charges levelled against the delinquent.

Thereafter, the management and delinquent have produced the witnesses and documents in support of their submissions and then, final award has been passed on 27.06.2014, in which the Tribunal has found that the enquiry is vitiated as the charges levelled against the delinquent are not found proved.

5. As per learned counsel for the petitioner-Bank, from the order of Tribunal i.e. Annexure-P/12, it is apparent that the orders of disciplinary authority and appellate authority were set-aside mainly on three grounds: firstly, that the delinquent was not supplied the list of witnesses and documents at the time of issuing charge-sheet; secondly, on 06.04.1993, photocopies of documents were filed by the representative of management in the proceedings and production of documents in piecemeal shows prejudice caused to the workman because before production of documents, some of the prosecution witnesses were already examined and as such, the principles of natural justice have not been followed; lastly, on the point that though a disagreement was shown by the disciplinary authority with the finding given by enquiry officer in respect of charge No.4 levelled against the delinquent, but since that disagreement did not contain any reason, therefore, the order passed by the disciplinary authority was not sustainable as it was contrary to the settled principle of law.
6.

Learned counsel for the petitioner-Bank has contended that the order passed by the Tribunal is not sustainable for the reason that the rule prevailing, does not provide any procedure that the documents and list of witnesses relied by the management should have been supplied at the time of issuing the charge-sheet.

He has further submitted that the documents and list of witnesses were supplied to the delinquent at a later point of time, but that does not cause any prejudice to him as no objection to that extent was ever raised by the delinquent during the course of enquiry.

He has further contended that though the documents could not be produced at the preliminary stage of enquiry and produced by the management at a later point of time even after recording the statement of some of the witnesses, but those witnesses were not relative with the documents produced by the management at a later point of time.

However, he has urged that after production of those documents, the relative witnesses were examined and as such, no prejudice was caused to the delinquent by producing the documents in piecemeal that too during the course of enquiry.

He has contended that so far as assigning reason for disagreement in respect of charge No.4 is concerned,
the same is not so material that it vitiates the whole order of disciplinary authority and that cannot be made a ground to set aside the order of disciplinary authority.

He has submitted that charge No.4 Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115496101/

sentences.text: was already not found proved by the disciplinary authority and that was not only the charge relating to the conduct of fraud and misappropriation of fund against the delinquent, whereas other three charges which were found proved and contained in the charge-sheet were relating to the conduct of fraud and misappropriation of fund of the Bank and also relating to manipulation and fabrication of documents.

He has also submitted that the finding of the Tribunal for setting-aside the order of disciplinary authority and also appellate authority only on the count that no reason was assigned by the disciplinary authority showing disagreement with regard to the finding of charge No.4, given by the enquiry officer is not proper, as such, the order of Tribunal is liable to be set-aside.

7. Learned counsel for the petitioner-Bank has also contended that even from the order passed by the Tribunal, it does not reveal that the disciplinary authority was satisfied with the point of disagreement in respect of charge No.4 only whereas the said charge is the only charge which was not completely found proved by the enquiry officer, but it was found partially proved on some of the points.

In support of his submissions, he has placed reliance upon the judgment reported (2018) 1 SCC 285 parties being Management of Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited Vs. M.Mani.
8.

sentences.text: Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-delinquent employee has opposed the submissions and submitted that the order passed by the Tribunal does not require to be interfered with.

He has contended that the charges levelled against the respondent were of serious nature and according to him, it is a settled principle of law that for proving serious charges, it was for the management to produce strict proof of evidence.

He has submitted that the allegation of fraud was also made against the present respondent and other employees, as such, criminal case was registered against them,
tried by the criminal Court, but on the same set of witnesses, the criminal Court has acquitted the respondent holding that he has not committed any sort of fraud.

The said judgment i.e. Exhibit-M/5 is available on record, upon which learned counsel for the respondent has placed reliance submitting that the Supreme Court in a recent judgment reported in (2024) 1 SCC 175 parties being Ram Lal Vs. State of Rajasthan & Others has observed that the finding of criminal Court is material and that still have a binding effect over other proceedings, if set of charges in other proceedings is same.

entities.text: Ram Lal Vs. State of Rajasthan & Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He has also submitted that the Bombay High Court in a case reported in (1985) 2 LLJ 145 parties being Jeevan Prakash Pandurang Mokashe Vs. State Bank of India and another has also dealt with the same situation and observed that the finding given by the criminal Court cannot be ignored by the disciplinary authority while charges are almost same in both the proceedings.

entities.text: Jeevan Prakash Pandurang Mokashe Vs. State Bank of India and another
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: He has also submitted that if appreciation of evidence of the witnesses adduced by the management, is done, then it is clear that none of the witnesses has alleged that any sort of financial loss was suffered by the customers or even by the Bank.

He has also contended that there was some procedural flaw committed in the petitioner-Bank which was found proved during the course of enquiry, but that cannot be a foundation for inflicting the punishment of dismissal, as such, the Tribunal rightly appreciating all the relevant facts and situations has set-aside the order of disciplinary authority and also the appellate authority.

He has also submitted that although the enquiry officer and disciplinary authority given the finding with regard to procedural flaw, but even otherwise from the evidence adduced, it is not clear that the respondent has committed any such type of irregularity or not followed the procedure prescribed in the Bank.

He has submitted that no charge has been found proved against the respondent and as such, the Tribunal appreciating the said aspect has rightly set-aside the orders of disciplinary authority and appellate authority which Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115496101/
3 does not call for any interference.

sentences.text: 9. Learned counsel for the respondent-delinquent has further submitted that the finding given by the Tribunal with regard to causing prejudice to the Bank is well appreciated and reasoned one.

He has contended that production of documents in the mid of enquiry otherwise causes prejudice to the employee, even though objection with regard to the said aspect has not been raised during the course of enquiry.
He has also submitted that if it is found that there was some procedural flaw on the part of the respondent, even then the punishment of dismissal is not proper.

10. Having heard the rival submissions of learned counsel for the parties and on perusal of relevant record especially the impugned award passed by the Tribunal, this Court is of the opinion that the Tribunal basically took note of the fact that a criminal case was also lodged against the respondent on the same set of facts, charges and with the same set of evidence and in which, the respondent was acquitted by the trial Court.

Though, the Tribunal in its award, has taken note of the fact that the present respondent and the Branch Manager against whom the departmental enquiry was initiated,
both have been dismissed from service, but in a criminal case registered against them, they were acquitted by the Court.

However, no document was produced by the petitioner-Bank neither before the Tribunal nor before this Court to indicate that the judgment passed by the trial Court has been further assailed or set-aside by any of the higher forum.
Thus, the Tribunal proceeded in the matter presuming that the judgment passed by the criminal Court in Case Nos.58/84 and 358/97 has attained finality.

The Tribunal has also appreciated the evidence adduced by the witnesses who were the witnesses in both the proceedings i.e. criminal case and departmental enquiry and after appreciating and comparing there statements and the view taken by the Court in criminal case, the Tribunal has also found that except Anil Shrivastava, the witness of the management, no other witness has been produced by the management.

The Tribunal has also, after making scrutiny of the statements of witnesses, arrived at a conclusion that the evidence of management witness is not cogent to prove the charge against the delinquent and after examining the overall circumstances and material produced by the prosecution, as per the Tribunal, there was no evidence that the amount shown debited was received by the workman/respondent.

11. Thus, before this Court, the sole issue which emerges to be decided is as to whether the Tribunal has committed any wrong in appreciating the validity of the order passed by the disciplinary authority comparing with the finding and view taken by the trial Court in a criminal case registered against the delinquent or not?

As per the award passed by the Tribunal, it is clear that the Tribunal has appreciated the evidentary value of material placed by the prosecution during the course of enquiry because as per the Tribunal, the departmental enquiry and criminal case both were based on same set of facts, evidence and charges.

The witnesses though secured their names in the list of witnesses produced by the prosecution and were also examined in the criminal case, but were not produced during the course of enquiry except one Anil Shrivastava, whose statement was very microscopically examined by the Tribunal and then arrived at a conclusion that the said witness has not said anything against the workman and his evidence is not sufficient to prove the charge against the workman.

sentences.text: Although, learned counsel for the petitioner-Bank has submitted that it is a settled principle of law that acquittal in criminal proceedings does not have a direct impact over the departmental proceedings because criminal proceedings are initiated by the State against the delinquent employee in a criminal Court, whereas departmental enquiry is initiated by the employer under Labour/Service Laws/Rules against the delinquent employee.

According to him, the employer conducted departmental enquiry in accordance with law independent of criminal case wherein charges against the delinquent employee was proved on the basis of preponderance of probabilities.

Dealing with this situation, the Supreme Court in the case of M. Mani (Supra) has observed as under:-
"17.

To begin with, when we examine the legality and the correctness of the awards of the Labour Court, we are of the considered opinion that the Labour Court, having held and indeed rightly that the departmental enquiry conducted by the appellant was legal and proper committed an error in holding that the departmental enquiry got vitiated due to criminal court's order which had acquitted the respondents from the charge of theft.
In our opinion, there was no occasion for the Labour Court to examine this issue once the departmental enquiry was held legal and proper.

The Labour Court, in our opinion, committed yet another error in holding that since the appellant failed to lead any evidence to prove the charge in Labour Court, therefore,
the dismissal orders of the respondents are liable to be set aside.
This finding, in our opinion, was again not legally sustainable.

18. In our opinion, once the Labour Court upheld the departmental enquiry as being legal and proper then the only question that survived for consideration before the Labour Court was whether the punishment of "dismissal" imposed by the appellant to the respondents was legal and proper or it requires any interference in its quantum.

19. In other words, the Labour Court should have then confined its enquiry to examine only one limited question as to whether the punishment given to the respondents, was, in any way, disproportionate to the gravity of the charge levelled against them and this, the Labour Court should have examined by taking recourse to the provisions of Section 11- A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short "the Act")
and the law laid down by this Court in Workmen v. Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. of

entities.text: Workmen v. Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. of
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: India (P) Ltd.
It was, however, not done thereby rendering the order of the Labour Court legally unsustainable."

Here in this case, the situation is altogether different that after passing the order by the Tribunal holding departmental enquiry to be vitiated on the ground of violation of principles of natural justice and directed the employer to lead evidence before the Tribunal itself.

The witness, namely,
Anil Shrivastava, was examined by the prosecution, but none other witness and, therefore, the Tribunal re-appreciated his statement with that of the finding given by the criminal Court in which also, Anil Shrivastava was one of the material witnesses and was examined by the criminal Court.

Thus, re-appreciation of evidence in a special circumstance existing in the present case by the Tribunal, cannot be said to be illegal because it is a witness who appeared before the Tribunal and as Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115496101/
5

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
such, the Tribunal was the authority which has to appreciate the reliability of the witness, therefore,
findings given by the Tribunal with regard to testimony of Anil Shrivastava, is not required to be re- examined by this Court in a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India preferred by the management.

13. However, the Tribunal in the present case, has compared the case of workman with that of criminal case registered against him for the reason that the witnesses in both the proceedings were same and the material produced by the prosecution in both the proceedings were also same and even the charges levelled against the workman were also same.

In this regard, the Supreme Court in a case reported in (2006) 5 SCC 446 parties being G.M. Tank Vs. State of Gujarat & Others has considered the fact that after acquittal in criminal trial, dismissal of an employee in departmental enquiry is not proper especially under the circumstances when there is no evidence against the employee to hold him guilty.

entities.text: G.M. Tank Vs. State of Gujarat & Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the said case, the Supreme Court has observed as under:-
"30.
The judgments relied on by the learned counsel appearing for the respondents are distinguishable on facts and on law.

In this case, the departmental proceedings and the criminal case are based on identical and similar set of facts and the charge in a departmental case against the appellant and the charge before the criminal court are one and the same.
It is true that the nature of charge in the departmental proceedings and in the criminal case is grave.

The nature of the case launched against the appellant on the basis of evidence and material collected against him during enquiry and investigation and as reflected in the charge-sheet, factors mentioned are one and the same.
In other words, charges, evidence, witnesses and circumstances are one and the same.

In the present case, criminal and departmental proceedings have already noticed or granted on the same set of facts, namely, raid conducted at the appellant's residence, recovery of articles therefrom.

The Investigating Officer Mr. V.B. Raval and other departmental witnesses were the only witnesses examined by the enquiry officer who by relying upon their statement came to the conclusion that the charges were established against the appellant.

The same witnesses were examined in the criminal case and the criminal court on the examination came to the conclusion that the prosecution has not proved the guilt alleged against the appellant beyond any reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant by its judicial pronouncement with the finding that the charge has not been proved.
It is also to be noticed that the judicial pronouncement was made after a regular trial and on hot contest.
Under these circumstances, it would be unjust and unfair and rather oppressive to allow the findings recorded in the departmental proceedings to stand.
31. In our opinion, such facts and evidence in the departmental as well as criminal proceedings were the same without there being any iota of difference, the appellant should succeed.
The distinction which is usually proved between the departmental and criminal proceedings on the basis of the approach and burden of proof would not be applicable in the instant case.

Though the finding recorded in the domestic enquiry was found to be valid by the courts below, when there was an honourable acquittal of the employee during the pendency of the proceedings challenging the Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115496101/
6 dismissal, the same requires to be taken note of and the decision in Paul Anthony case will apply.

entities.text: Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We, therefore, hold that the appeal filed by the appellant deserves to be allowed. "

Likewise, in the case of Ram Lal (Supra), the Supreme Court has observed that :-
"25.
With this above background, if we examine the criminal proceedings the following factual position emerges.
The very same witnesses, who were examined in the departmental enquiry were examined in the criminal trial.

Jagdish Chandra,
Bhawani Singh, Shravan Lal, Raj Singh and Karan Sharma were examined as PW2,
PW3, PW6, PW9 and PW13 respectively at the criminal trial.
Apart from them, eight other witnesses were also examined.

The gravamen of the charge in the criminal case was that the appellant had submitted an application for recruitment along with his marksheet and he, by making alteration in his date of birth to reflect the same as 24.04.1972 in place of 21.04.1974, and obtained recruitment to the post of Constable.
26.
Though the Trial Court convicted the appellant under Section 420 of IPC, the Appellate Court recorded the following crucial findings while acquitting the appellant:
"...Mainly the present case was based on the documents to this effect whether the date of birth of accused is 21.04.1972 or 21.04.1974.
Exh. P-3 is original Marksheet, in which, the date of birth of accused has been shown as 21.04.1972 and same has also been proved by the witnesses examined on behalf of the prosecution.
Whatever the documents have been produced before the Court regarding the date of birth of 21.04.1974 are either the letters of Principal or are Duplicate T.C. or Marksheets.

Neither the prosecution has produced any such original documents in the Subordinate Court to this effect that when the admission form of accused was filled,
what date of birth was mentioned by the accused in it, what was the date of birth in Roll Register of School, what date of birth was mentioned by accused in the Examination Form of Secondary, and nor after bringing the original records from the concerned witnesses concerned, same were got proved in the evidence.
In these circumstances, this fact becomes doubtful that date of birth of accused was 21.04.1974, and accused is entitled to receive it's benefit.
In the considered opinion of this Court, the conviction made by the Ld. Subordinate Court merely on the basis of oral evidence and letters or duplicate documents, is not just and proper.
It is justifiable to acquit the accused.

Resultantly, on the basis of aforesaid consideration,
the present appeal filed by the Appellant-Accused is liable to be allowed. "
[Emphasis supplied]

27. What is important to notice is that the Appellate Judge has clearly recorded that in the document Exh. P-3 - original marksheet of the 8th standard, the date of birth was clearly shown as 21.04.1972 and the other documents produced by the prosecution were either letters or a duplicate marksheet.

Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115496101/
7

entities.text: Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: No doubt, the Appellate Judge says that it becomes doubtful whether the date of birth was 21.04.1974 and that the accused was entitled to receive its benefit.
However, what we are supposed to see is the substance of the judgment.

A reading of the entire judgment clearly indicates that the appellant was acquitted after full consideration of the prosecution evidence and after noticing that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the charge [See S. Samuthiram]
28.
Expressions like "benefit of doubt" and "honorably acquitted", used in judgments are not to be understood as magic incantations.
A court of law will not be carried away by the mere use of such terminology.

In the present case, the Appellate Judge has recorded that Exh. P-3, the original marksheet carries the date of birth as 21.04.1972 and the same has also been proved by the witnesses examined on behalf of the prosecution.

The conclusion that the acquittal in the criminal proceeding was after full consideration of the prosecution evidence and that the prosecution miserably failed to prove the charge can only be arrived at after a reading of the judgment in its entirety.
The court in judicial review is obliged to examine the substance of the judgment and not go by the form of expression used.

29. We are satisfied that the findings of the Appellate Judge in the criminal case clearly indicate that the charge against the appellant was not just, "not proved" - in fact the charge even stood "disproved" by the very prosecution evidence.

As held by this Court, a fact is said to be "disproved"
when, after considering the matters before it, the court either believes that it does not exist or considers its non-existence so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that it does not exist.

A fact is said to be "not proved"
when it is neither "proved" nor "disproved" [See Vijayee Singh and Others v. State of U.P. (1990) 3 SCC 190].
30.

entities.text: Vijayee Singh and Others v. State of U.P. (1990) 3 SCC 190
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We are additionally satisfied that in the teeth of the finding of the Appellate Judge, the disciplinary proceedings and the orders passed thereon cannot be allowed to stand.
The charges were not just similar but identical and the evidence, witnesses and circumstances were all the same.
This is a case where in exercise of our discretion, we quash the orders of the disciplinary authority and the appellate authority as allowing them to stand will be unjust, unfair and oppressive.

This case is very similar to the situation that arose in G.M. Tank (supra).
31.
Apart from the above, one other aspect is to be noted.
The Enquiry Officer's report makes a reference to the appellant passing 10th standard, and to a 10th standard marksheet exhibited as Exh. P-4 referring to the date of birth as 24.07.1974.
Jagdish Chandra-PW1 (in the departmental enquiry) clearly deposed that since the appellant was regularly absent from Class 10, his name was struck off and he did not even pass 10th standard.
The appellant has also come out with this version before the disciplinary authority, stating that the 10th class certificate of Ram Lal produced before the Enquiry Officer, is of some other Ram Lal.
32. This issue need not detain us any further because it is not the case of department that the appellant sought employment based on 10th standard marksheet.
It is their positive case that the appellant sought employment on the basis of his 8th standard marksheet.

Shravan Lal-PW- 4 in the departmental enquiry had also furnished the 10th standard marksheet procured from the Secondary Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115496101/

entities.text: Secondary Madhyanchal Gramin Bank vs Jinesh Kumar Kothia
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 8 Education Board, Ajmer.
In cross-examination, on being asked, he admitted that the appellant was recruited on the basis of 8th standard marksheet, and he admitted that there was no alteration in the 8th standard marksheet.

33. In view of the above, we declare that the order of termination dated 31.03.2004; the order of the Appellate Authority dated 08.10.2004; the orders dated 29.03.2008 and 25.06.2008 refusing to reconsider and review the penalty respectively, are all illegal and untenable. "

When the Tribunal has considered this aspect that the sole witness of management,
namely, Anil Shrivastava, has also been examined in the criminal case and his evidence was not found sufficient by the trial Court to hold the accused guilty of charges levelled, therefore, in absence of any other material witness produced by the prosecution, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that evidence adduced by the management is not sufficient to prove the charge levelled against the workman.

14. Learned counsel for the petitioner has also challenged the order dated 20.04.2010 which was the initial order passed by the Tribunal holding the enquiry initiated by the department against the workman is in violation of principles of natural justice and as such, directed the Bank to produce the evidence in relation to alleged irregularity so as to prove misconduct against the delinquent.

However, as per learned counsel for the petitioner, the enquiry conducted by the employer was found invalid on the ground that at the time of supplying the charge- sheet, the documents and list of witnesses referred in the charge-sheet were not supplied to the delinquent.

According to him, so far as charge No.4 which was not found proved is concerned,
since that charge was not so grave and does not make any direct impact over the conduct of the delinquent because other charges which were serious in nature, were found proved by the enquiry officer, therefore, the observation made by the Tribunal with regard to procedure adopted by the management for conducting the enquiry,
held to be improper by the Tribunal, was not correct.

However, I am of the opinion that when charge No.4 undisputably not found proved by the enquiry officer in its report, then disciplinary authority went wrong while passing the order inflicting punishment holding charge No.4 to have been found proved without issuing any show-cause to the delinquent showing its disagreement with regard to the finding of enquiry officer whereby he has observed that charge No.4 was not found proved.

The enquiry in that regard, was held to be invalid as it was in violation of principles of natural justice because law provides that if disciplinary authority disagrees with the finding of enquiry officer, he should have given an opportunity to the delinquent issuing notice specifying the reason of disagreement in the notice itself.

So far as the submission of learned counsel for the petitioner that charge No.4 is not so grave and its impact over the final order is not that much, which makes the whole enquiry vitiated is concerned

, I am of the opinion that the charges found proved against the delinquent may be grave but the overall impact of the view of the disciplinary authority has to be examined when order of punishment is put for test and as such,
the order passed by the Tribunal, in my opinion, cannot be held illegal.

sentences.text:
After considering the view of the Tribunal in the light of the law laid-down by the Supreme Court and taking into account the fact that when the Tribunal has very meticulously considered the gravity of evidence produced during the course of enquiry granting opportunity to the management to lead evidence despite that they chose not to produce any witness except Anil Shrivastava before it, in my opinion, the order passed by the Tribunal does not need any interference and at the same time, if the view of the Supreme Court as has been considered above, is taken note of vis-a-viz with the finding of the trial Court acquitting the respondent and also the Manager of the Bank, the submissions made by learned counsel for the petitioner do not influence me to dislodge the finding given by the Tribunal and as such, this petition, being without any substance, is hereby, dismissed.

The same witnesses were examined in the criminal case and the criminal court on the examination came to the conclusion that the prosecution has not proved the guilt alleged against the appellant beyond any reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant by its judicial pronouncement with the finding that the charge has not been proved.
It is also to be noticed that the judicial pronouncement was made after a regular trial and on hot contest.
Under these circumstances, it would be unjust and unfair and rather oppressive to allow the findings recorded in the departmental proceedings to stand.
The distinction which is usually proved between the departmental and criminal proceedings on the basis of the approach and burden of proof would not be applicable in the instant case.

A reading of the entire judgment clearly indicates that the appellant was acquitted after full consideration of the prosecution evidence and after noticing that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove the charge [See S. Samuthiram]
28.
Expressions like "benefit of doubt" and "honorably acquitted", used in judgments are not to be understood as magic incantations.
A court of law will not be carried away by the mere use of such terminology.
In the present case, the Appellate Judge has recorded that Exh. P-3, the original marksheet carries the date of birth as 21.04.1972 and the same has also been proved by the witnesses examined on behalf of the prosecution.
The conclusion that the acquittal in the criminal proceeding was after full consideration of the prosecution evidence and that the prosecution miserably failed to prove the charge can only be arrived at after a reading of the judgment in its entirety.
The court in judicial review is obliged to examine the substance of the judgment and not go by the form of expression used.
29. We are satisfied that the findings of the Appellate Judge in the criminal case clearly indicate that the charge against the appellant was not just, "not proved" - in fact the charge even stood "disproved" by the very prosecution evidence.
As held by this Court, a fact is said to be "disproved"
when, after considering the matters before it, the court either believes that it does not exist or considers its non-existence so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that it does not exist.
A fact is said to be "not proved"
when it is neither "proved" nor "disproved" [See Vijayee Singh and Others v. State of U.P. (1990) 3 SCC 190].
30.
We are additionally satisfied that in the teeth of the finding of the Appellate Judge, the disciplinary proceedings and the orders passed thereon cannot be allowed to stand.
The charges were not just similar but identical and the evidence, witnesses and circumstances were all the same.
This is a case where in exercise of our discretion, we quash the orders of the disciplinary authority and the appellate authority as allowing them to stand will be unjust, unfair and oppressive.
